taxonomy.subtopic: Hypoxemia from hypoventilation versus V/Q mismatch

questions.stem_html: A 29-year-old man is found somnolent after taking an unknown medication. He breathes 6 times/min. On room air at sea level, arterial blood gas shows pH 7.24, PCO2 70 mm Hg, and PO2 54 mm Hg. The respiratory quotient is 0.8. Which additional finding is most likely?

options.text_html: A normal alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient that improves with ventilation
A widened alveolar-arterial gradient caused by diffusion limitation
A widened gradient caused by an intracardiac right-to-left shunt
A normal gradient that fails to improve with restoration of ventilation
An elevated alveolar PO2 caused by reduced carbon dioxide excretion

questions.explanation_html: At sea level, alveolar PO2 is approximately 150 − (70/0.8) = 62.5 mm Hg, giving an A–a gradient of about 9 mm Hg. This normal gradient indicates pure alveolar hypoventilation: both alveolar and arterial PO2 fall together. Restoring ventilation lowers PCO2 and raises alveolar and arterial oxygen.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Diffusion limitation increases the A–a gradient because alveolar oxygen does not equilibrate with capillary blood.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: A right-to-left shunt widens the gradient and responds incompletely to supplemental oxygen.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Hypoxemia from hypoventilation corrects when alveolar ventilation is restored.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Increasing alveolar PCO2 lowers, rather than raises, alveolar PO2 in the alveolar gas equation.

questions.educational_objective: Use the alveolar gas equation to identify a normal A–a gradient in isolated hypoventilation.

media.alt_text: Alveolar gas equation and normal A-a gradient during hypoventilation.

taxonomy.subtopic: Opposing DLCO effects of emphysema and polycythemia

questions.stem_html: A 62-year-old man with a 45-pack-year smoking history has exertional dyspnea, hyperinflation, and decreased breath sounds. His hematocrit is 60% because of chronic hypoxemia. Compared with another patient who has equally severe emphysematous destruction but a normal hematocrit, how will the measured diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide most likely differ?

options.text_html: It will be lower because erythrocytosis thickens the alveolar-capillary membrane
It may be relatively higher because additional hemoglobin binds more carbon monoxide
It will be identical because DLCO is independent of hemoglobin concentration
It will normalize because polycythemia restores destroyed alveolar surface area
It will become immeasurable because carbon monoxide cannot cross emphysematous alveoli

questions.explanation_html: Emphysema lowers DLCO by destroying alveolar surface area. Polycythemia independently raises measured DLCO because more hemoglobin is available to bind transferred carbon monoxide. Thus severe emphysema still impairs diffusion, but the measured value can be higher than expected unless corrected for hemoglobin.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Erythrocytosis increases red-cell mass without thickening the alveolar-capillary membrane.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: DLCO depends on hemoglobin concentration and should be corrected for anemia or polycythemia.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: More hemoglobin cannot restore lost alveolar septa or surface area.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Remaining alveoli still transfer carbon monoxide; emphysema reduces rather than abolishes DLCO.

questions.educational_objective: Recognize hemoglobin concentration as a modifier of measured DLCO that can partially mask emphysematous surface-area loss.

media.alt_text: Competing effects of alveolar surface loss and increased hemoglobin on DLCO.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 5, 2026.

questions.stem_html: A patient with emphysema performs a forced expiration from total lung capacity. Despite greater expiratory effort, airflow reaches a plateau. Loss of elastic recoil causes the equal-pressure point to move toward smaller, noncartilaginous airways. Which change most directly explains the flow limitation?

options.text_html: Increased surfactant production raises small-airway surface tension
Increased radial traction keeps bronchioles open throughout expiration
Pleural pressure exceeds intraluminal pressure earlier along collapsible airways
Alveolar pressure becomes lower than atmospheric pressure during forced expiration
Cartilage hypertrophy narrows the terminal bronchioles

questions.explanation_html: During forced expiration, pleural pressure becomes positive and airway pressure falls toward the mouth. Reduced elastic recoil lowers the driving pressure within the airway, so the equal-pressure point shifts distally into unsupported bronchioles. Beyond that point, pleural pressure exceeds airway pressure and produces dynamic compression; extra effort raises both pressures and cannot restore flow.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Surfactant lowers surface tension and is not the cause of expiratory airway collapse in emphysema.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Emphysema destroys radial traction, making small airways less stable.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Alveolar pressure must exceed atmospheric pressure for expiratory flow.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Terminal bronchioles lack cartilage; emphysema causes loss of support rather than cartilage hypertrophy.

questions.educational_objective: Explain effort-independent expiratory flow limitation in emphysema by distal movement of the equal-pressure point into collapsible airways.

media.alt_text: Airway pressure decline and dynamic compression at the equal-pressure point.

questions.stem_html: A mechanically ventilated patient is studied at different static lung volumes while cardiac output and alveolar oxygen concentration are held constant. Pulmonary vascular resistance is lowest near functional residual capacity but rises at both residual volume and total lung capacity. Which vascular changes explain this U-shaped relationship?

options.text_html: Alveolar vessels narrow at low volume, whereas extra-alveolar vessels narrow at high volume
Both vascular groups dilate progressively as lung volume increases
Alveolar vessels are compressed at high volume, whereas extra-alveolar vessels lose radial traction at low volume
Extra-alveolar vessels are compressed by alveoli only at functional residual capacity
Hypoxic vasoconstriction is maximal at both volume extremes despite constant alveolar oxygen

questions.explanation_html: At high lung volumes, expanded alveoli compress capillaries within alveolar walls. At low lung volumes, reduced parenchymal radial traction allows extra-alveolar vessels to narrow. The opposing vessel behaviors make total pulmonary vascular resistance lowest near functional residual capacity and higher at both extremes.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: This reverses the vessel groups affected at the two extremes.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Alveolar capillaries are compressed rather than dilated at high lung volume.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Extra-alveolar vessels are best supported near normal lung volume and narrow as radial traction falls.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Alveolar oxygen was held constant, so hypoxic vasoconstriction cannot explain the curve.

questions.educational_objective: Relate lung volume to opposite changes in alveolar and extra-alveolar vessel resistance.

media.alt_text: U-shaped pulmonary vascular resistance curve across lung volumes.

taxonomy.subtopic: Hypoxemia from low-V/Q units after flow redistribution

questions.stem_html: A 54-year-old woman develops sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea 5 days after knee replacement. CT angiography shows an embolus occluding a segmental pulmonary artery. The obstructed alveoli remain ventilated. Nevertheless, arterial oxygen tension falls. Which mechanism best accounts for the hypoxemia?

options.text_html: Carbon dioxide retention from complete loss of total minute ventilation
Blood is redirected to remaining lung regions, creating low-V/Q units that incompletely oxygenate it
The embolized region becomes a true right-to-left shunt
Pulmonary capillary blood equilibrates with an abnormally low inspired oxygen tension
Hemoglobin loses its ability to bind oxygen after platelet activation

questions.explanation_html: The embolized region has high V/Q (dead space), because it is ventilated but not perfused. Redistribution of blood to unaffected regions can lower their V/Q ratios, and blood leaving these units is incompletely oxygenated. This V/Q heterogeneity, plus reduced mixed venous oxygen in some patients, produces hypoxemia.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Minute ventilation is usually maintained or increased; hypocapnia is common.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: A ventilated but unperfused region is dead space, not a shunt.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Inspired oxygen tension is not lowered by an intravascular embolus.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Platelet activation does not abolish hemoglobin oxygen binding.

questions.educational_objective: Explain pulmonary-embolism hypoxemia through perfusion redistribution and low-V/Q regions despite dead space at the obstruction.

media.alt_text: Perfusion redistribution from a dead-space unit to low-VQ lung units.

taxonomy.subtopic: Genome-segment reassortment in a coinfected host

questions.stem_html: Respiratory illness spreads rapidly across several continents. The causal influenza A strain contains a hemagglutinin subtype not recently circulating in humans. Genetic analysis shows that several RNA segments closely resemble an avian strain and the remaining segments resemble a human strain. Which event most directly generated this virus?

options.text_html: Accumulation of point mutations during error-prone RNA replication
Integration of viral complementary DNA into a host chromosome
Homologous recombination between two nonsegmented RNA genomes
Reassortment of genome segments in a cell coinfected by distinct influenza A viruses
Acquisition of a bacterial plasmid encoding hemagglutinin

questions.explanation_html: Influenza A has eight negative-sense RNA segments. Coinfection of one host cell by distinct strains allows progeny virions to package new combinations of segments. This reassortment can abruptly change surface antigens—antigenic shift—and create pandemic potential when population immunity is low.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Gradual point mutation causes antigenic drift, not the abrupt mixed-segment pattern described.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Influenza replicates without a DNA intermediate or chromosomal integration.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: The defining mechanism is segment reassortment, not homologous recombination of nonsegmented genomes.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Viruses do not acquire hemagglutinin through bacterial plasmids.

questions.educational_objective: Identify influenza A segment reassortment as the molecular basis of antigenic shift.

media.alt_text: Two segmented influenza genomes reassorting inside one host cell.

questions.stem_html: A 17-year-old boy with sickle cell disease develops fever, hypotension, and meningismus. Blood culture grows an alpha-hemolytic, optochin-sensitive gram-positive diplococcus. The loss of which splenic function most strongly predisposed him to this fulminant infection?

options.text_html: Negative selection of autoreactive T cells
Production of secretory IgA by mucosal plasma cells
Removal of circulating immune complexes by hepatic Kupffer cells
Activation of eosinophils against tissue-invasive helminths
Opsonization-dependent phagocytic clearance of encapsulated bacteria from blood

questions.explanation_html: Repeated splenic infarction causes functional asplenia in sickle cell disease. Splenic macrophages and marginal-zone B-cell responses are especially important for clearing opsonized encapsulated organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae. Without this filtering function, bacteremia can progress rapidly to sepsis and meningitis.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Central T-cell negative selection occurs in the thymus.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Mucosal IgA production is not the principal splenic defense lost here.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Kupffer cells reside in the liver, and their function is not removed by autosplenectomy.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Helminth defense depends largely on Th2 responses, IgE, and eosinophils rather than splenic filtration.

questions.educational_objective: Link functional asplenia to impaired blood-borne clearance of opsonized encapsulated bacteria.

media.alt_text: Splenic filtration of opsonized encapsulated bacteria from blood.

taxonomy.subtopic: Gs alpha ADP-ribosylation and persistent adenylate cyclase activation

questions.stem_html: A 31-year-old aid worker develops profuse painless watery diarrhea after drinking contaminated water. Stool contains no leukocytes. The bacterial toxin responsible enters enterocytes and covalently modifies a G-protein alpha subunit. Which intracellular change follows directly?

options.text_html: Persistent activation of phospholipase C with increased IP3
Inactivation of the Gs alpha GTPase, causing sustained adenylate cyclase activity
Inhibition of the 60S ribosomal subunit by cleavage of 28S rRNA
Blockade of acetylcholine release by SNARE protein cleavage
Activation of guanylate cyclase by a heat-stable peptide

questions.explanation_html: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gs alpha and prevents its intrinsic GTPase activity, locking it in the active GTP-bound state. Persistent adenylate cyclase activity raises cAMP, activates CFTR-mediated chloride secretion, and drives sodium and water into the intestinal lumen.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Gq-linked signaling activates phospholipase C; cholera toxin targets Gs.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Shiga toxin and Shiga-like toxin injure the 60S ribosomal subunit.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins and blocks acetylcholine release.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: ETEC heat-stable toxin activates guanylate cyclase and increases cGMP.

questions.educational_objective: Trace cholera toxin ADP-ribosylation of Gs alpha to persistent cAMP-mediated secretory diarrhea.

media.alt_text: Cholera toxin signaling from Gs alpha to cAMP and chloride secretion.

taxonomy.subtopic: Th1-mediated caseating granulomas and apical cavitation

questions.stem_html: A 44-year-old man has weight loss, night sweats, hemoptysis, and an upper-lobe cavitary lesion. Sputum contains acid-fast bacilli. Lung biopsy shows caseating granulomas. Which immune pathway is most directly responsible for both containment of the organism and much of the tissue injury?

options.text_html: Th2 secretion of interleukin-4 with eosinophil recruitment
Cytotoxic T-cell secretion of interleukin-10 with macrophage deactivation
Th17 suppression of neutrophil migration through interleukin-17
Th1 secretion of interferon-gamma with macrophage activation and delayed hypersensitivity
B-cell class switching to IgE with mast-cell degranulation

questions.explanation_html: Mycobacterial antigens drive IL-12-dependent Th1 differentiation. Th1-derived interferon-gamma activates macrophages, promoting intracellular killing and granuloma formation. The same type IV delayed hypersensitivity response contributes to caseation, necrosis, and cavitary tissue damage.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Th2 and eosinophilic responses are characteristic of helminths and allergy.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: IL-10 is anti-inflammatory and deactivates macrophages rather than forming effective granulomas.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: IL-17 promotes rather than suppresses neutrophil recruitment and is not the defining pathway here.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: IgE-mediated mast-cell activation causes immediate hypersensitivity, not caseating granulomas.

questions.educational_objective: Connect Th1 interferon-gamma signaling to macrophage activation, granuloma containment, and type IV tissue injury in tuberculosis.

media.alt_text: Th1 macrophage activation leading to granuloma formation and caseation.

references.citation: USMLE. Step 1 Exam Content Outline and Specifications. Accessed August 5, 2026.

taxonomy.subtopic: Viridans streptococcal adherence to damaged valves

questions.stem_html: A 38-year-old man with a known bicuspid aortic valve develops 3 weeks of low-grade fever and fatigue after a dental extraction. Blood cultures grow alpha-hemolytic, optochin-resistant cocci. Which microbial property most facilitates infection of the abnormal valve?

options.text_html: Coagulase-mediated conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin
Polysaccharide dextran-mediated adherence to platelet-fibrin deposits
M protein-mediated inhibition of complement deposition
Protein A binding to the Fc portion of IgG
A polysaccharide capsule composed of polyribosylribitol phosphate

questions.explanation_html: Viridans streptococci can enter the bloodstream after dental manipulation. Dextrans promote adherence to platelet-fibrin aggregates on previously damaged endocardium, producing a relatively indolent native-valve endocarditis.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Coagulase is a major Staphylococcus aureus virulence factor.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Protein A is produced by Staphylococcus aureus.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: The polyribosylribitol phosphate capsule belongs to Haemophilus influenzae type b.

questions.educational_objective: Identify dextran-mediated adherence as a viridans streptococcal mechanism for colonizing damaged valves after transient bacteremia.

media.alt_text: Viridans streptococci adhering to a platelet-fibrin deposit on damaged endocardium.
